_comment: UK operator. Tuned for ~£400 of working capital. The binding constraint is not margin, it is how long cash stays tied up in an item that has not sold.

thresholds._comment: maxAskCents caps a single buy at £100 so no one item can take more than a quarter of the float. minRoi is high because with small capital, percentage return per turn matters far more than absolute profit: $40 on a $60 buy beats $60 on a $300 buy, because the first one can be run four times.

economics._comment: A wider buffer than the 5% default. One bad unit hurts far more when the float is $500, and the buffer is what absorbs a return, a scuff missed in the photos, or a shipping surprise.

weights._comment: Velocity is weighted above raw profit. Capital that turns over twice a month at 60% beats capital that turns once a quarter at 120%.

freight._comment: Off. Freight items are the classic way to lose a whole float on one sofa.

pace._comment: Deliberately modest. A slow monitor that keeps the Facebook account alive is worth more than a fast one that gets checkpointed.

location._comment: Facebook's Marketplace location is account state, not a URL parameter, so a city slug is a request rather than a guarantee. Every listing's country is checked; anything outside GB is dropped before it costs a model call.

alerts._comment: Near misses are sent too, clearly labelled as not-a-buy. Silence is ambiguous: without them there is no way to tell a thin market from a broken scraper from thresholds set too tight.
